finding.claim: The /invoice/<inv_id> route returns any invoice with no ownership check (IDOR / broken access control). The sibling /my/invoice route enforces inv['customer'] == g.user['id'], so the missing check looks like an oversight.
finding.source: The inv_id URL path parameter, supplied by any requester. The route has no authentication or ownership precondition, so unauthenticated callers can use it too.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, including the customer field and any other invoice data.

trace.note: Route /invoice/<inv_id> is registered with no auth decorator.
INVOICES.get(inv_id) looks up the invoice by the caller-supplied ID only. It does not use g.user.
The record is returned to the caller without comparing inv['customer'] to the requesting user.

finding.guards_checked: No authorization check on this route. It never reads g.user, and there is no decorator and no before_request hook in the file. The sibling route at invoices.py:16 does compare inv['customer'] with g.user['id'] and returns 404 on mismatch, which confirms the intended policy. Enumerating invoice IDs is feasible if they are sequential or guessable.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no decorator or before_request hook, looks up INVOICES.get(inv_id) and returns jsonify(inv) without reading g.user, while the sibling at invoices.py:16 does enforce inv["customer"] == g.user["id"], so any anonymous caller who knows or guesses an ID gets the invoice.

verdict_facts.reason: invoices.py:7-10 returns INVOICES.get(inv_id) via jsonify with no auth decorator, no g.user comparison and no before_request hook, whereas the sibling route at invoices.py:16 does check inv["customer"] != g.user["id"]. invoices.py is the only file in the directory.
